值得閱讀的理由

  • 從中共官方「國家安全」的定義切入，深入解析政權最核心關切的安全排序與內部邏輯。
  • 剖析外部大國（如美國）的戰略施壓，為何可能在威權體制下被轉化為凝聚民族主義的內部護盾。
  • 探討同為華語文化圈的中華民國（台灣）民主轉型經驗，對中共一黨體制治理正當性所形成的深層制度對比。

摘要

權力核心的思考實驗：外部威脅與內部政治安全

影片中，說故事的人（阿牛）提出一項思想實驗：若北京高層同時面對美軍印太軍演、中華民國自由選舉以及中國各大城市爆發大規模內部抗議三份緊急通報，何者最具關鍵威脅？作者引述中共官方發布的國家安全文件指出，北京明確將政治安全視為國家安全的生命線，其核心即為維護政權安全與制度安全。這顯示比起外部軍事或經濟壓力，能夠直接觸及執政地位與制度存續的因素，才是其政策衡量的重中之重。

外部制衡的局限：美國壓力與民族主義轉化

針對美國的戰略施壓，作者分析指出，美國無疑在軍事、科技、金融及全球盟友網絡上擁有最強實力，並對北京實施全面戰略防堵。然而，強大的外在對手往往是一把雙刃劍；當威權體制面臨房地產疲軟或就業不足等內部經濟挑戰時，外部制裁與遏制容易被轉化為「外敵打壓崛起」的政治敘事，從而激發民族主義，使內部治理壓力轉向一致對外，甚至為強化言論審查與維穩機制提供合理化藉口。

文化與體制的對照：台灣民主經驗的參照意義

至於中華民國（台灣）的定位，作者認為除了領土訴求與第一島鏈的地緣戰略價值之外，最深層的影響在於治理體制的對比。台灣同屬華語社會並深受中華文化影響，同樣經歷過戒嚴與威權時期，但最終透過解除戒嚴、國會全面改選與總統直選，達成了和平政黨輪替。這種由威權走向民主制度的歷史路徑，向外界證明了華人社會實踐憲政民主的可行性，進而構成強烈的體制參照。

================================================

What if one day the people said, "Thank you, Communist Party, for all you have done, but for the next term, we’d like to switch to another party—is that possible?" >> Suppose 100 million people in mainland China dislike the Communist Party today , but they are all isolated at home, don't know each other, and have no media , no unions, no parties, no leaders, no funding, and no idea that their neighbors feel the same—then the threat they pose to the CCP might not be as great as people imagine. But what about another scenario? There are only one million people, but they know of each other's existence, have cross-platform communication, organizations, resources, and shared demands—some officials within the system are even willing to talk to them. Then everything changes, because from that moment on, discontent is no longer just an emotion; it becomes a political force. People often ask about the map behind me; this map is not just the Republic of China that I dream of, but the way the Republic of China should look in the hearts of 1.4 billion descendants of the Middle Kingdom. With. the goal of restoring the Republic of China, we are carrying out the mission of national recovery and rebuilding the republic using the Three Principles of the People, and we have launched a map poster. With our merchandise bundle of map tapestries, map pillows, and Republic of China flag keychains—kids choose, but I want them all! You can take them all home for just 1911. And now, shipping is free on both platforms on orders over 699. Friends overseas don't need to worry; we will launch an international purchasing plan soon, so hurry up and get yours! Hello everyone, I'm A-Niu. Today, let's conduct a very interesting thought experiment: suppose Zhongnanhai receives three urgent reports tonight at the same time. The. first report says the U.S. has sent an aircraft carrier strike group into the Western Pacific and is conducting large-scale military exercises with the Philippines. The second report says the Republic of China’s free areas have completed another free election, and the new ruling party does not support "One Country, Two Systems." The third report says large-scale protests have erupted simultaneously in over a dozen major Chinese cities, including Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Chengdu, and Wuhan , with students, workers, the middle class, and even some civil servants. demanding political reform. If you were the top leader of the CCP today, which report would keep you awake at night? The United States, the Republic of China , or the Chinese people? Many might instinctively choose the United States, as it is one of the world's most powerful military, financial, and technological forces, backed by a global alliance system. Others might choose the Republic of China, because for decades, Beijing has maintained high-intensity political and military pressure regarding the Taiwan. issue, even linking national unification to national rejuvenation. But what if the question today isn't who has the most power to harm the CCP, but who is most likely to truly end the CCP's one-party rule? The answer might be completely different , and this isn't just a guess of mine; the CCP's own official documents have already provided the answer to some extent. In 2025, the CCP authorities released a white paper on China's national security.

in the new era. This document is very interesting because it's not a foreign scholar's analysis of the CCP, but the CCP itself telling everyone what they truly consider most important. The white paper clearly states that China's national security must be based on political security, further stating that political security is the lifeline of national security. So, what is political security? The document answers directly: the core of political security is regime security and systemic security, and the most. fundamental aspect is safeguarding the leadership and governing position of the Chinese Communist Party. Notice that it doesn't list economic security, military security, or territorial. security first, but rather political security. Even Article 3 of the 2015 National Security Law of the People's Republic of China explicitly states that it is based on political security. So, if you really want to understand what the CCP fears most, there is a simple method: don't just look at how many missiles the PLA has, or who the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is scolding. every day. You need to look at what directly threatens the Communist Party's rule; that is the true core of this entire video. Let's first talk about the United States . If asked today, which foreign country has the most ability to exert strategic pressure on the CCP? The U.S. is undoubtedly number one, because the U.S. has many cards to play: militarily, it has powerful naval and air forces with global bases, and allies in Asia like Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines ; technologically, the U.S. still holds. immense influence in AI, semiconductors , aerospace, software, and research; financially, it has the dollar system; and diplomatically, it has a global alliance network. So, what can the United States do? It can restrict the CCP's access to certain advanced technologies, raise tariffs, adjust supply chains, strengthen military deployments in the Indo-Pacific, cooperate with Japan, Australia, and the Philippines, and increase the costs for Beijing to engage in military adventurism over the Taiwan issue. So if you ask which foreign country the. CCP fears most, there is really no suspense: it's the U.S. But there is a very interesting point here. The U.S. is very strong, but it may not be the force most likely to directly end the CCP regime. Because an external enemy has a very strange characteristic : it can sometimes actually help an authoritarian regime consolidate its domestic power. Think about it: if the mainland's economy is struggling today—with a real estate slump, youth unemployment, and bottlenecks in tech development— normally, people might start asking if the government's policies are to blame. But at that moment, if the US increases sanctions on the CCP, the CCP gains a very convenient narrative to use. They can claim it’s not their fault, but that the US doesn't want China to rise; that we can't buy semiconductors, that the US is strangling our supply chain, that the West is containing China, causing international relations to sour , and that US hegemony is suppressing the Chinese people. As a result, the anger that should have been directed at the government can be diverted outward, ultimately turning into a narrative that the nation is being bullied by foreigners and that we.

must stand united. This is where nationalism becomes extremely useful for an authoritarian regime. That is why we discussed in our previous video that greater external pressure does not necessarily mean an authoritarian regime will democratize faster; sometimes, the opposite is true. The greater the external pressure, the easier it is for the regime to justify maintaining stability, censoring speech, militarizing, and even demanding that everyone stop discussing politics and unite against a common enemy. So, while the US is indeed a very powerful external adversary to the CCP, if the US. were to directly go to war with the CCP , it might actually allow the CCP to tell its billions of people: "Look, we are truly being invaded by foreign powers." In such a scenario, they might even reap short-term dividends from a surge in nationalism. In short, the US can weaken the CCP's power, but the existence of an external enemy can also provide the CCP with a democratic shield. Next, let's talk about the free area of the Republic of China. If we only look at Beijing’s political propaganda over the past few decades, we find that. Taiwan is almost always ranked as one of the most sensitive topics. The Taiwan issue white paper released by the CCP's State Council in 2022 directly tied national reunification to national rejuvenation, while once again refusing to renounce the use of force. So, why is Taiwan so important? Many would say it’s because of territory, and that is certainly the first layer. The CCP has long defined Taiwan as an unfinished national unification issue. If Taiwan refuses to accept Beijing's rule, then the national rejuvenation. they claim will always remain incomplete . The second layer is military and geopolitical strategy; Taiwan sits in a crucial position along the first island chain in the Western Pacific, and its geography directly impacts the strategic space of China, the East China Sea, the South China Sea, and the Pacific. But there is a third layer, which I think is the most interesting part: the system itself. The most troublesome aspect of this region is that its people can truly choose the government they want through the ballot box. Let’s be clear here: the Beijing authorities have never written a single. line saying "we are afraid of Taiwan's democracy," so we cannot write that script for them. However, from the perspective of systemic comparison, the existence of the Republic of China on Taiwan does indeed provide a very interesting political contrast. Because Taiwan is not a Western country; it uses the same Chinese language, is deeply influenced by Chinese culture, and, like the mainland, was not free and democratic from the start. We went through martial law, one-party rule, press censorship, and an authoritarian era, but what was the final result? Martial law was lifted, the parliament. was fully re-elected, the president was directly elected by the people, different parties began competing for central power, and in 2000, the first peaceful transfer of power between the ruling party and the opposition was achieved. The official historical records of the Presidential Office of the Republic of China also list the 2000 transfer of power as Taiwan's first peaceful party rotation. So, Taiwan has at least proven one thing: a Chinese-speaking society does not have to rely on one-party dictatorship to function. This point creates a very awkward problem for Beijing's political narrative. You can tell the Chinese.

people that "Western democracy is not suited for China; the American system is too chaotic, and European culture is different from China." But the most troublesome part about Taiwan is that Taiwanese people are not Americans, and the Republic of China's democratic system was not air-dropped from Washington. It is a historical path that evolved from modern Chinese revolutionary republican constitutionalism to Taiwan, where it eventually achieved democratization. Of course, I am absolutely not saying that the democratic experience of Taiwan's 20 million people can be directly replicated in mainland China with its. 1.4 billion people—the scale, history, and regional differences are all completely different—but it at least refutes a very simple and crude argument : that Chinese culture is inherently unsuited for democracy. If it is inherently unsuited, then what is Taiwan today? This is why the Taiwan issue is so complex for the CCP. It is simultaneously a territorial issue , a nationalist issue, a U.S.-China competition issue, a strategic issue, and also, to a small extent, a comparative systems issue. But even so, it is very difficult for Taiwan itself. to directly overthrow the CCP; Taiwan’s 20 million people cannot go to the mainland to vote for over a billion people, nor can they decide for the mainland people whether the mainland should continue its one-party dictatorship. Therefore, what Taiwan can truly provide is more of an alternative possibility, which is to tell everyone that Chinese society does not have only one political path, and Chinese history does not have to be a choice between only emperors and the Communist Party. But whether this possibility ultimately. becomes the institutional reality of mainland China is something only the mainland people themselves can decide. Speaking of this, you may have already guessed that if the United States cannot directly establish democracy for the mainland, and Taiwan cannot directly vote for the people of the mainland. Then the ones who truly have the ability to end one-party rule in the end are still the people of the mainland themselves. However, I must add one more sentence here: it is not the case that the CCP will fall just because the mainland people are dissatisfied. If it were that simple, it would have already collapsed during the Great Leap Forward era. What truly matters is whether the. people have transitioned from being " discontented individuals" into a " political entity"; there is a vast difference between the two. After all, one complaining person may not be as dangerous as one million organized people. Suppose there are 100 million people in mainland China today who... dislike the Communist Party, but these 100 million people are all at home, don't know each other, lack media, unions, political parties, leaders, funding, and don't even know that their next-door neighbor thinks the same way; then the political threat these 100 million people pose to the CCP might not be as great as everyone imagines,. because they are merely many isolated malcontents. But what if the situation were different? What if there were only one million people, but these one million knew of each other's existence, had cross-platform communication, organization, resources, common demands , and even some officials within the system willing to talk to them? Then things would be completely different. So, I think we can summarize what the CCP truly fears in one simple sentence: it's not 100 million discontented people , but one million people who know they are all discontented and know what to do.

next. Because from that moment on, discontent is no longer just an emotion; it begins to transform into a political force. And this point isn't just something I, Niu Ge, imagined; the 2025 CCP National Security White Paper explicitly states the need to strictly prevent so-called " color revolutions" and street politics, and even explicitly mentions avoiding the spread of various non-political risks into political risks. This statement is worth thinking about carefully: what does it mean for non-political risks to spread into political risks? For example, it starts. with unfinished buildings, where everyone just wants their homes—that's an economic issue. But when owners of unfinished buildings from different cities start connecting, they begin to ask why banks lent the money out in the first place? Why did local government oversight fail ? Why does everyone have the same problem ? Eventually, everyone realizes this might not just be a problem with one specific developer, and that’s when economic issues start to become politicized. The same applies to workers demanding back pay; one factory failing to pay. wages is just a labor dispute, but if workers in 100 cities suddenly start asking, "Why are we all facing the same systemic issues?" then everything changes. Therefore, what the CCP truly fears is not the people encountering problems, but the people beginning to link different problems into a single political issue. Here we must discuss what is truly worth studying about the 1989 Democracy Movement. It is not just about how many students were in Tiananmen Square, but about several dangerous factors converging in mainland China that year:. first, social discontent due to inflation and other issues; second, the rapid expansion of the student movement ; third, the involvement of workers and citizens, not just students; fourth, protests spreading beyond Beijing to cities like Shanghai, Chengdu, and Guangzhou; and most dangerously, the fifth factor: a split within the top leadership of the CCP, leading to conflicting opinions. Zhao Ziyang and others favored dialogue and a moderate approach, while another group of top leaders believed the movement posed a direct threat to the Party’s rule and. that hardline measures were necessary. Historical records from the U.S. State Department also indicate that there were clear divisions among the CCP leadership at the time regarding how to handle the situation. This is why 1989 was so dangerous; it wasn’t because the students in the square suddenly became stronger than the PLA, but because the cracks in society outside almost connected with the cracks in power within the Party. This is the scenario a regime truly fears. But what finally resolved 1989? The answer is the gun. In the end, the hardliners in the CCP. gained the upper hand, martial law troops entered Beijing, Zhao Ziyang lost power, and the protests were suppressed by force. So, this teaches us that even if people take to the streets, even if the movement spans across cities, and even if there is a split within the Party, as long as the military, the public security, and the police remain obedient, the regime can still hold on. This is why the CCP has always placed such great importance on the "Party commanding the gun," because once the gun no longer belongs to the Party, the nature of a political crisis changes completely. I have always felt that the.

moment many authoritarian regimes truly fear most is not when people first shout for them to step down, but when a supreme leader orders a crackdown one day, and the soldiers stand their ground , with some even saying, "I will not fire this time." At that moment, the regime truly faces its end. Here, we can piece together the real answer of this video: the U.S. is strong, but the CCP won't necessarily fall just from U.S. pressure. The Republic of China is sensitive, but Taiwan’s democracy has existed for decades, and the CCP has not collapsed because of it. The people of. mainland China may be very dissatisfied , but if that dissatisfaction lacks organization, the regime can still continue to exist. The truly dangerous combination is an economic or social crisis, large-scale public discontent, the beginning of organized opposition forces, top CCP elites splitting, some bureaucrats starting to pick sides, and the military and police beginning to hesitate at suppression orders. At that point, the situation becomes completely different. So if one must ask who the CCP fears most, I think the most accurate answer is not simply the people of mainland China, but a public that is organized,. has shared political demands, gains support from within the system, and causes the coercive apparatus to hesitate. Only then do the people truly transform from the ruled into political sovereigns . I don’t want to go to the other extreme here, either, by saying the CCP doesn’t actually fear the U.S. or that the ROC isn’t important. That’s certainly not the case. The U.S. can change the external environment for China’s democratization, provide international information, balance the CCP’s external expansion, exert diplomatic pressure on human rights. issues, and raise the costs for the CCP regime to engage in external military adventures. But the U.S. cannot build democracy for 1.4 billion Chinese, and the ROC cannot choose the ruling party for the people on the mainland. Because if the mainland’s political system were ever decided directly by Washington, what would that have to do with popular sovereignty? Similarly, Taiwan can offer a very precious experience in democratization. We can tell our friends on the mainland that authoritarianism is not incapable of ending; the Kuomintang was also a long-term ruling party, yet it was still. able to lift the ban on political parties and hold comprehensive parliamentary elections. We were also able to hold direct presidential elections and hand over power peacefully . So, Taiwan proves that another path truly exists. But Taiwan cannot vote for the mainland people. Therefore, what the U.S. can do is change the external conditions, and what Taiwan can do is provide a structural reference, but the only people who can ultimately decide the mainland’s system are the mainland people themselves. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 從中共官方「國家安全」的定義切入，深入解析政權最核心關切的安全排序與內部邏輯。
  • 剖析外部大國（如美國）的戰略施壓，為何可能在威權體制下被轉化為凝聚民族主義的內部護盾。
  • 探討同為華語文化圈的中華民國（台灣）民主轉型經驗，對中共一黨體制治理正當性所形成的深層制度對比。

摘要

權力核心的思考實驗：外部威脅與內部政治安全

影片中，說故事的人（阿牛）提出一項思想實驗：若北京高層同時面對美軍印太軍演、中華民國自由選舉以及中國各大城市爆發大規模內部抗議三份緊急通報，何者最具關鍵威脅？作者引述中共官方發布的國家安全文件指出，北京明確將政治安全視為國家安全的生命線，其核心即為維護政權安全與制度安全。這顯示比起外部軍事或經濟壓力，能夠直接觸及執政地位與制度存續的因素，才是其政策衡量的重中之重。

外部制衡的局限：美國壓力與民族主義轉化

針對美國的戰略施壓，作者分析指出，美國無疑在軍事、科技、金融及全球盟友網絡上擁有最強實力，並對北京實施全面戰略防堵。然而，強大的外在對手往往是一把雙刃劍；當威權體制面臨房地產疲軟或就業不足等內部經濟挑戰時，外部制裁與遏制容易被轉化為「外敵打壓崛起」的政治敘事，從而激發民族主義，使內部治理壓力轉向一致對外，甚至為強化言論審查與維穩機制提供合理化藉口。

文化與體制的對照：台灣民主經驗的參照意義

至於中華民國（台灣）的定位，作者認為除了領土訴求與第一島鏈的地緣戰略價值之外，最深層的影響在於治理體制的對比。台灣同屬華語社會並深受中華文化影響，同樣經歷過戒嚴與威權時期，但最終透過解除戒嚴、國會全面改選與總統直選，達成了和平政黨輪替。這種由威權走向民主制度的歷史路徑，向外界證明了華人社會實踐憲政民主的可行性，進而構成強烈的體制參照。

================================================

What if one day the people said, "Thank you, Communist Party, for all you have done, but for the next term, we’d like to switch to another party—is that possible?" >> Suppose 100 million people in mainland China dislike the Communist Party today , but they are all isolated at home, don't know each other, and have no media , no unions, no parties, no leaders, no funding, and no idea that their neighbors feel the same—then the threat they pose to the CCP might not be as great as people imagine. Then everything changes, because from that moment on, discontent is no longer just an emotion; it becomes a political force. People often ask about the map behind me; this map is not just the Republic of China that I dream of, but the way the Republic of China should look in the hearts of 1.4 billion descendants of the Middle Kingdom. With. the goal of restoring the Republic of China, we are carrying out the mission of national recovery and rebuilding the republic using the Three Principles of the People, and we have launched a map poster. With our merchandise bundle of map tapestries, map pillows, and Republic of China flag keychains—kids choose, but I want them all! You can take them all home for just 1911. And now, shipping is free on both platforms on orders over 699. Friends overseas don't need to worry; we will launch an international purchasing plan soon, so hurry up and get yours! Hello everyone, I'm A-Niu. Today, let's conduct a very interesting thought experiment: suppose Zhongnanhai receives three urgent reports tonight at the same time. The. first report says the U.S. has sent an aircraft carrier strike group into the Western Pacific and is conducting large-scale military exercises with the Philippines. The second report says the Republic of China’s free areas have completed another free election, and the new ruling party does not support "One Country, Two Systems." If you were the top leader of the CCP today, which report would keep you awake at night? The United States, the Republic of China , or the Chinese people? Many might instinctively choose the United States, as it is one of the world's most powerful military, financial, and technological forces, backed by a global alliance system. in the new era. This document is very interesting because it's not a foreign scholar's analysis of the CCP, but the CCP itself telling everyone what they truly consider most important. The white paper clearly states that China's national security must be based on political security, further stating that political security is the lifeline of national security. So, what is political security? The document answers directly: the core of political security is regime security and systemic security, and the most. fundamental aspect is safeguarding the leadership and governing position of the Chinese Communist Party. Notice that it doesn't list economic security, military security, or territorial. security first, but rather political security. Even Article 3 of the 2015 National Security Law of the People's Republic of China explicitly states that it is based on political security. So, if you really want to understand what the CCP fears most, there is a simple method: don't just look at how many missiles the PLA has, or who the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is scolding. every day. You need to look at what directly threatens the Communist Party's rule; that is the true core of this entire video. Let's first talk about the United States . If asked today, which foreign country has the most ability to exert strategic pressure on the CCP? The U.S. is undoubtedly number one, because the U.S. has many cards to play: militarily, it has powerful naval and air forces with global bases, and allies in Asia like Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines ; technologically, the U.S. still holds. immense influence in AI, semiconductors , aerospace, software, and research; financially, it has the dollar system; and diplomatically, it has a global alliance network. So, what can the United States do? It can restrict the CCP's access to certain advanced technologies, raise tariffs, adjust supply chains, strengthen military deployments in the Indo-Pacific, cooperate with Japan, Australia, and the Philippines, and increase the costs for Beijing to engage in military adventurism over the Taiwan issue. So if you ask which foreign country the. CCP fears most, there is really no suspense: it's the U.S. But there is a very interesting point here. The U.S. is very strong, but it may not be the force most likely to directly end the CCP regime. Because an external enemy has a very strange characteristic : it can sometimes actually help an authoritarian regime consolidate its domestic power. Think about it: if the mainland's economy is struggling today—with a real estate slump, youth unemployment, and bottlenecks in tech development— normally, people might start asking if the government's policies are to blame. But at that moment, if the US increases sanctions on the CCP, the CCP gains a very convenient narrative to use. They can claim it’s not their fault, but that the US doesn't want China to rise; that we can't buy semiconductors, that the US is strangling our supply chain, that the West is containing China, causing international relations to sour , and that US hegemony is suppressing the Chinese people. As a result, the anger that should have been directed at the government can be diverted outward, ultimately turning into a narrative that the nation is being bullied by foreigners and that we.

must stand united. This is where nationalism becomes extremely useful for an authoritarian regime. That is why we discussed in our previous video that greater external pressure does not necessarily mean an authoritarian regime will democratize faster; sometimes, the opposite is true. The greater the external pressure, the easier it is for the regime to justify maintaining stability, censoring speech, militarizing, and even demanding that everyone stop discussing politics and unite against a common enemy. So, while the US is indeed a very powerful external adversary to the CCP, if the US. were to directly go to war with the CCP , it might actually allow the CCP to tell its billions of people: "Look, we are truly being invaded by foreign powers." In such a scenario, they might even reap short-term dividends from a surge in nationalism. In short, the US can weaken the CCP's power, but the existence of an external enemy can also provide the CCP with a democratic shield. Next, let's talk about the free area of the Republic of China. If we only look at Beijing’s political propaganda over the past few decades, we find that. Taiwan is almost always ranked as one of the most sensitive topics. The Taiwan issue white paper released by the CCP's State Council in 2022 directly tied national reunification to national rejuvenation, while once again refusing to renounce the use of force. So, why is Taiwan so important? Many would say it’s because of territory, and that is certainly the first layer. The CCP has long defined Taiwan as an unfinished national unification issue. If Taiwan refuses to accept Beijing's rule, then the national rejuvenation. they claim will always remain incomplete . The second layer is military and geopolitical strategy; Taiwan sits in a crucial position along the first island chain in the Western Pacific, and its geography directly impacts the strategic space of China, the East China Sea, the South China Sea, and the Pacific. But there is a third layer, which I think is the most interesting part: the system itself. The most troublesome aspect of this region is that its people can truly choose the government they want through the ballot box. Let’s be clear here: the Beijing authorities have never written a single. line saying "we are afraid of Taiwan's democracy," so we cannot write that script for them. However, from the perspective of systemic comparison, the existence of the Republic of China on Taiwan does indeed provide a very interesting political contrast. Because Taiwan is not a Western country; it uses the same Chinese language, is deeply influenced by Chinese culture, and, like the mainland, was not free and democratic from the start. We went through martial law, one-party rule, press censorship, and an authoritarian era, but what was the final result? Martial law was lifted, the parliament. was fully re-elected, the president was directly elected by the people, different parties began competing for central power, and in 2000, the first peaceful transfer of power between the ruling party and the opposition was achieved. The official historical records of the Presidential Office of the Republic of China also list the 2000 transfer of power as Taiwan's first peaceful party rotation. So, Taiwan has at least proven one thing: a Chinese-speaking society does not have to rely on one-party dictatorship to function. This point creates a very awkward problem for Beijing's political narrative. You can tell the Chinese.

people that "Western democracy is not suited for China; the American system is too chaotic, and European culture is different from China." But the most troublesome part about Taiwan is that Taiwanese people are not Americans, and the Republic of China's democratic system was not air-dropped from Washington. It is a historical path that evolved from modern Chinese revolutionary republican constitutionalism to Taiwan, where it eventually achieved democratization. Of course, I am absolutely not saying that the democratic experience of Taiwan's 20 million people can be directly replicated in mainland China with its. 1.4 billion people—the scale, history, and regional differences are all completely different—but it at least refutes a very simple and crude argument : that Chinese culture is inherently unsuited for democracy. If it is inherently unsuited, then what is Taiwan today? This is why the Taiwan issue is so complex for the CCP. It is simultaneously a territorial issue , a nationalist issue, a U.S.-China competition issue, a strategic issue, and also, to a small extent, a comparative systems issue. But even so, it is very difficult for Taiwan itself. to directly overthrow the CCP; Taiwan’s 20 million people cannot go to the mainland to vote for over a billion people, nor can they decide for the mainland people whether the mainland should continue its one-party dictatorship. Therefore, what Taiwan can truly provide is more of an alternative possibility, which is to tell everyone that Chinese society does not have only one political path, and Chinese history does not have to be a choice between only emperors and the Communist Party. But whether this possibility ultimately. becomes the institutional reality of mainland China is something only the mainland people themselves can decide. Speaking of this, you may have already guessed that if the United States cannot directly establish democracy for the mainland, and Taiwan cannot directly vote for the people of the mainland. Then the ones who truly have the ability to end one-party rule in the end are still the people of the mainland themselves. However, I must add one more sentence here: it is not the case that the CCP will fall just because the mainland people are dissatisfied. If it were that simple, it would have already collapsed during the Great Leap Forward era. What truly matters is whether the. people have transitioned from being " discontented individuals" into a " political entity"; there is a vast difference between the two. After all, one complaining person may not be as dangerous as one million organized people. Suppose there are 100 million people in mainland China today who... dislike the Communist Party, but these 100 million people are all at home, don't know each other, lack media, unions, political parties, leaders, funding, and don't even know that their next-door neighbor thinks the same way; then the political threat these 100 million people pose to the CCP might not be as great as everyone imagines,. because they are merely many isolated malcontents. But what if the situation were different? What if there were only one million people, but these one million knew of each other's existence, had cross-platform communication, organization, resources, common demands , and even some officials within the system willing to talk to them? Then things would be completely different. So, I think we can summarize what the CCP truly fears in one simple sentence: it's not 100 million discontented people , but one million people who know they are all discontented and know what to do.

next. Because from that moment on, discontent is no longer just an emotion; it begins to transform into a political force. And this point isn't just something I, Niu Ge, imagined; the 2025 CCP National Security White Paper explicitly states the need to strictly prevent so-called " color revolutions" and street politics, and even explicitly mentions avoiding the spread of various non-political risks into political risks. This statement is worth thinking about carefully: what does it mean for non-political risks to spread into political risks? For example, it starts. with unfinished buildings, where everyone just wants their homes—that's an economic issue. But when owners of unfinished buildings from different cities start connecting, they begin to ask why banks lent the money out in the first place? Why did local government oversight fail ? Why does everyone have the same problem ? Eventually, everyone realizes this might not just be a problem with one specific developer, and that’s when economic issues start to become politicized. The same applies to workers demanding back pay; one factory failing to pay. wages is just a labor dispute, but if workers in 100 cities suddenly start asking, "Why are we all facing the same systemic issues?" then everything changes. Therefore, what the CCP truly fears is not the people encountering problems, but the people beginning to link different problems into a single political issue. Here we must discuss what is truly worth studying about the 1989 Democracy Movement. It is not just about how many students were in Tiananmen Square, but about several dangerous factors converging in mainland China that year:. first, social discontent due to inflation and other issues; second, the rapid expansion of the student movement ; third, the involvement of workers and citizens, not just students; fourth, protests spreading beyond Beijing to cities like Shanghai, Chengdu, and Guangzhou; and most dangerously, the fifth factor: a split within the top leadership of the CCP, leading to conflicting opinions. Zhao Ziyang and others favored dialogue and a moderate approach, while another group of top leaders believed the movement posed a direct threat to the Party’s rule and. that hardline measures were necessary. Historical records from the U.S. State Department also indicate that there were clear divisions among the CCP leadership at the time regarding how to handle the situation. This is why 1989 was so dangerous; it wasn’t because the students in the square suddenly became stronger than the PLA, but because the cracks in society outside almost connected with the cracks in power within the Party. This is the scenario a regime truly fears. But what finally resolved 1989? The answer is the gun. In the end, the hardliners in the CCP. gained the upper hand, martial law troops entered Beijing, Zhao Ziyang lost power, and the protests were suppressed by force. So, this teaches us that even if people take to the streets, even if the movement spans across cities, and even if there is a split within the Party, as long as the military, the public security, and the police remain obedient, the regime can still hold on. This is why the CCP has always placed such great importance on the "Party commanding the gun," because once the gun no longer belongs to the Party, the nature of a political crisis changes completely. I have always felt that the.

moment many authoritarian regimes truly fear most is not when people first shout for them to step down, but when a supreme leader orders a crackdown one day, and the soldiers stand their ground , with some even saying, "I will not fire this time." At that moment, the regime truly faces its end. Here, we can piece together the real answer of this video: the U.S. is strong, but the CCP won't necessarily fall just from U.S. pressure. The Republic of China is sensitive, but Taiwan’s democracy has existed for decades, and the CCP has not collapsed because of it. The people of. mainland China may be very dissatisfied , but if that dissatisfaction lacks organization, the regime can still continue to exist. does not mean the ruling party is necessarily terrible, nor does it mean that the Communist Party would definitely lose if it participated in an election. Over 100 years ago , when our Founding Father discussed the Three Principles of the People, he was already pondering that a government must be capable, or else the nation cannot be governed. That is why our Founding Father emphasized that political power belongs to the people, while the government. possesses administrative power. People can entrust administrative work to a professional government, but in the end , who is the master? It is still the people. Revolution to the democratization of the Republic of China today, Chinese people have been walking for over 100 years to answer the question of who the country actually belongs to. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 從中共官方「國家安全」的定義切入，深入解析政權最核心關切的安全排序與內部邏輯。
  • 剖析外部大國（如美國）的戰略施壓，為何可能在威權體制下被轉化為凝聚民族主義的內部護盾。
  • 探討同為華語文化圈的中華民國（台灣）民主轉型經驗，對中共一黨體制治理正當性所形成的深層制度對比。

摘要

權力核心的思考實驗：外部威脅與內部政治安全

影片中，說故事的人（阿牛）提出一項思想實驗：若北京高層同時面對美軍印太軍演、中華民國自由選舉以及中國各大城市爆發大規模內部抗議三份緊急通報，何者最具關鍵威脅？作者引述中共官方發布的國家安全文件指出，北京明確將政治安全視為國家安全的生命線，其核心即為維護政權安全與制度安全。這顯示比起外部軍事或經濟壓力，能夠直接觸及執政地位與制度存續的因素，才是其政策衡量的重中之重。

外部制衡的局限：美國壓力與民族主義轉化

針對美國的戰略施壓，作者分析指出，美國無疑在軍事、科技、金融及全球盟友網絡上擁有最強實力，並對北京實施全面戰略防堵。然而，強大的外在對手往往是一把雙刃劍；當威權體制面臨房地產疲軟或就業不足等內部經濟挑戰時，外部制裁與遏制容易被轉化為「外敵打壓崛起」的政治敘事，從而激發民族主義，使內部治理壓力轉向一致對外，甚至為強化言論審查與維穩機制提供合理化藉口。

文化與體制的對照：台灣民主經驗的參照意義

至於中華民國（台灣）的定位，作者認為除了領土訴求與第一島鏈的地緣戰略價值之外，最深層的影響在於治理體制的對比。台灣同屬華語社會並深受中華文化影響，同樣經歷過戒嚴與威權時期，但最終透過解除戒嚴、國會全面改選與總統直選，達成了和平政黨輪替。這種由威權走向民主制度的歷史路徑，向外界證明了華人社會實踐憲政民主的可行性，進而構成強烈的體制參照。

================================================

What if one day the people said, "Thank you, Communist Party, for all you have done, but for the next term, we’d like to switch to another party—is that possible?" >> Suppose 100 million people in mainland China dislike the Communist Party today , but they are all isolated at home, don't know each other, and have no media , no unions, no parties, no leaders, no funding, and no idea that their neighbors feel the same—then the threat they pose to the CCP might not be as great as people imagine. But what about another scenario? There are only one million people, but they know of each other's existence, have cross-platform communication, organizations, resources, and shared demands—some officials within the system are even willing to talk to them. Then everything changes, because from that moment on, discontent is no longer just an emotion; it becomes a political force. People often ask about the map behind me; this map is not just the Republic of China that I dream of, but the way the Republic of China should look in the hearts of 1.4 billion descendants of the Middle Kingdom. With. the goal of restoring the Republic of China, we are carrying out the mission of national recovery and rebuilding the republic using the Three Principles of the People, and we have launched a map poster. With our merchandise bundle of map tapestries, map pillows, and Republic of China flag keychains—kids choose, but I want them all! You can take them all home for just 1911. And now, shipping is free on both platforms on orders over 699. Friends overseas don't need to worry; we will launch an international purchasing plan soon, so hurry up and get yours! Hello everyone, I'm A-Niu. Today, let's conduct a very interesting thought experiment: suppose Zhongnanhai receives three urgent reports tonight at the same time. The. first report says the U.S. has sent an aircraft carrier strike group into the Western Pacific and is conducting large-scale military exercises with the Philippines. The second report says the Republic of China’s free areas have completed another free election, and the new ruling party does not support "One Country, Two Systems." The third report says large-scale protests have erupted simultaneously in over a dozen major Chinese cities, including Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Chengdu, and Wuhan , with students, workers, the middle class, and even some civil servants. demanding political reform. If you were the top leader of the CCP today, which report would keep you awake at night? The United States, the Republic of China , or the Chinese people? Many might instinctively choose the United States, as it is one of the world's most powerful military, financial, and technological forces, backed by a global alliance system. Others might choose the Republic of China, because for decades, Beijing has maintained high-intensity political and military pressure regarding the Taiwan. issue, even linking national unification to national rejuvenation. But what if the question today isn't who has the most power to harm the CCP, but who is most likely to truly end the CCP's one-party rule? In 2025, the CCP authorities released a white paper on China's national security.

in the new era. This document is very interesting because it's not a foreign scholar's analysis of the CCP, but the CCP itself telling everyone what they truly consider most important. The white paper clearly states that China's national security must be based on political security, further stating that political security is the lifeline of national security. So, what is political security? The document answers directly: the core of political security is regime security and systemic security, and the most. fundamental aspect is safeguarding the leadership and governing position of the Chinese Communist Party. Notice that it doesn't list economic security, military security, or territorial. security first, but rather political security. Even Article 3 of the 2015 National Security Law of the People's Republic of China explicitly states that it is based on political security. So, if you really want to understand what the CCP fears most, there is a simple method: don't just look at how many missiles the PLA has, or who the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is scolding. every day. You need to look at what directly threatens the Communist Party's rule; that is the true core of this entire video. Let's first talk about the United States . If asked today, which foreign country has the most ability to exert strategic pressure on the CCP? The U.S. is undoubtedly number one, because the U.S. has many cards to play: militarily, it has powerful naval and air forces with global bases, and allies in Asia like Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines ; technologically, the U.S. still holds. immense influence in AI, semiconductors , aerospace, software, and research; financially, it has the dollar system; and diplomatically, it has a global alliance network. So, what can the United States do? It can restrict the CCP's access to certain advanced technologies, raise tariffs, adjust supply chains, strengthen military deployments in the Indo-Pacific, cooperate with Japan, Australia, and the Philippines, and increase the costs for Beijing to engage in military adventurism over the Taiwan issue. So if you ask which foreign country the. CCP fears most, there is really no suspense: it's the U.S. But there is a very interesting point here. The U.S. is very strong, but it may not be the force most likely to directly end the CCP regime. Because an external enemy has a very strange characteristic : it can sometimes actually help an authoritarian regime consolidate its domestic power. Think about it: if the mainland's economy is struggling today—with a real estate slump, youth unemployment, and bottlenecks in tech development— normally, people might start asking if the government's policies are to blame. But at that moment, if the US increases sanctions on the CCP, the CCP gains a very convenient narrative to use. They can claim it’s not their fault, but that the US doesn't want China to rise; that we can't buy semiconductors, that the US is strangling our supply chain, that the West is containing China, causing international relations to sour , and that US hegemony is suppressing the Chinese people. As a result, the anger that should have been directed at the government can be diverted outward, ultimately turning into a narrative that the nation is being bullied by foreigners and that we.

must stand united. This is where nationalism becomes extremely useful for an authoritarian regime. That is why we discussed in our previous video that greater external pressure does not necessarily mean an authoritarian regime will democratize faster; sometimes, the opposite is true. The greater the external pressure, the easier it is for the regime to justify maintaining stability, censoring speech, militarizing, and even demanding that everyone stop discussing politics and unite against a common enemy. So, while the US is indeed a very powerful external adversary to the CCP, if the US. were to directly go to war with the CCP , it might actually allow the CCP to tell its billions of people: "Look, we are truly being invaded by foreign powers." In such a scenario, they might even reap short-term dividends from a surge in nationalism. In short, the US can weaken the CCP's power, but the existence of an external enemy can also provide the CCP with a democratic shield. Next, let's talk about the free area of the Republic of China. If we only look at Beijing’s political propaganda over the past few decades, we find that. Taiwan is almost always ranked as one of the most sensitive topics. The Taiwan issue white paper released by the CCP's State Council in 2022 directly tied national reunification to national rejuvenation, while once again refusing to renounce the use of force. So, why is Taiwan so important? Many would say it’s because of territory, and that is certainly the first layer. The CCP has long defined Taiwan as an unfinished national unification issue. If Taiwan refuses to accept Beijing's rule, then the national rejuvenation. they claim will always remain incomplete . The second layer is military and geopolitical strategy; Taiwan sits in a crucial position along the first island chain in the Western Pacific, and its geography directly impacts the strategic space of China, the East China Sea, the South China Sea, and the Pacific. But there is a third layer, which I think is the most interesting part: the system itself. The most troublesome aspect of this region is that its people can truly choose the government they want through the ballot box. Let’s be clear here: the Beijing authorities have never written a single. line saying "we are afraid of Taiwan's democracy," so we cannot write that script for them. However, from the perspective of systemic comparison, the existence of the Republic of China on Taiwan does indeed provide a very interesting political contrast. Because Taiwan is not a Western country; it uses the same Chinese language, is deeply influenced by Chinese culture, and, like the mainland, was not free and democratic from the start. We went through martial law, one-party rule, press censorship, and an authoritarian era, but what was the final result? Martial law was lifted, the parliament. was fully re-elected, the president was directly elected by the people, different parties began competing for central power, and in 2000, the first peaceful transfer of power between the ruling party and the opposition was achieved. The official historical records of the Presidential Office of the Republic of China also list the 2000 transfer of power as Taiwan's first peaceful party rotation. So, Taiwan has at least proven one thing: a Chinese-speaking society does not have to rely on one-party dictatorship to function. This point creates a very awkward problem for Beijing's political narrative. You can tell the Chinese.

people that "Western democracy is not suited for China; the American system is too chaotic, and European culture is different from China." But the most troublesome part about Taiwan is that Taiwanese people are not Americans, and the Republic of China's democratic system was not air-dropped from Washington. It is a historical path that evolved from modern Chinese revolutionary republican constitutionalism to Taiwan, where it eventually achieved democratization. Of course, I am absolutely not saying that the democratic experience of Taiwan's 20 million people can be directly replicated in mainland China with its. 1.4 billion people—the scale, history, and regional differences are all completely different—but it at least refutes a very simple and crude argument : that Chinese culture is inherently unsuited for democracy. If it is inherently unsuited, then what is Taiwan today? This is why the Taiwan issue is so complex for the CCP. It is simultaneously a territorial issue , a nationalist issue, a U.S.-China competition issue, a strategic issue, and also, to a small extent, a comparative systems issue. But even so, it is very difficult for Taiwan itself. to directly overthrow the CCP; Taiwan’s 20 million people cannot go to the mainland to vote for over a billion people, nor can they decide for the mainland people whether the mainland should continue its one-party dictatorship. Therefore, what Taiwan can truly provide is more of an alternative possibility, which is to tell everyone that Chinese society does not have only one political path, and Chinese history does not have to be a choice between only emperors and the Communist Party. But whether this possibility ultimately. becomes the institutional reality of mainland China is something only the mainland people themselves can decide. Speaking of this, you may have already guessed that if the United States cannot directly establish democracy for the mainland, and Taiwan cannot directly vote for the people of the mainland. Then the ones who truly have the ability to end one-party rule in the end are still the people of the mainland themselves. However, I must add one more sentence here: it is not the case that the CCP will fall just because the mainland people are dissatisfied. If it were that simple, it would have already collapsed during the Great Leap Forward era. What truly matters is whether the. people have transitioned from being " discontented individuals" into a " political entity"; there is a vast difference between the two. After all, one complaining person may not be as dangerous as one million organized people. Suppose there are 100 million people in mainland China today who... dislike the Communist Party, but these 100 million people are all at home, don't know each other, lack media, unions, political parties, leaders, funding, and don't even know that their next-door neighbor thinks the same way; then the political threat these 100 million people pose to the CCP might not be as great as everyone imagines,. because they are merely many isolated malcontents. But what if the situation were different? What if there were only one million people, but these one million knew of each other's existence, had cross-platform communication, organization, resources, common demands , and even some officials within the system willing to talk to them? Then things would be completely different. So, I think we can summarize what the CCP truly fears in one simple sentence: it's not 100 million discontented people , but one million people who know they are all discontented and know what to do.

next. Because from that moment on, discontent is no longer just an emotion; it begins to transform into a political force. And this point isn't just something I, Niu Ge, imagined; the 2025 CCP National Security White Paper explicitly states the need to strictly prevent so-called " color revolutions" and street politics, and even explicitly mentions avoiding the spread of various non-political risks into political risks. This statement is worth thinking about carefully: what does it mean for non-political risks to spread into political risks? For example, it starts. with unfinished buildings, where everyone just wants their homes—that's an economic issue. But when owners of unfinished buildings from different cities start connecting, they begin to ask why banks lent the money out in the first place? Why did local government oversight fail ? Here we must discuss what is truly worth studying about the 1989 Democracy Movement. This is why 1989 was so dangerous; it wasn’t because the students in the square suddenly became stronger than the PLA, but because the cracks in society outside almost connected with the cracks in power within the Party.
